title: 10+ years in gamedev, the last year and a half making games with AI. This one is 23 days old: a sky-islands sandbox with airships you design and shoot apart, on a custom C++ engine, built almost entirely by AI.
author: I_GRIN_I
selftext:
I've been making games for over 10 years, and for the last year and a half I've been making them with AI. 23 days ago I started this one from an empty folder, and almost everything in the video was built by AI. My part is game design, architecture, art direction and testing. I haven't written a line of code myself.

The game is called Feraloft. It's a sandbox of floating islands. On an island you build your own village and settle the creatures you've captured there (capture isn't in this video yet). They work for you, gathering resources and keeping production going, while you fly on to the next island, in another biome, to set up production of some new material. To get there you design your own airship piece by piece in a shipyard editor (frame, hull, guns, engines, balloons), build it, and fight other ships on the way. Hits knock real pieces off, and a ship can break apart and fall out of the sky. There are also caves, dungeons and wings for gliding.

Long term I want it to grow into a colony sim: your islands link up into a network, your ships carry cargo between the colonies, and it all turns into one big empire that produces everything.

There's no Unity, Unreal or Godot here. It's a custom C++ engine on SDL3, with Jolt for physics, Vulkan on Windows and Metal on macOS, and it builds on Linux too. The same shaders run on Vulkan and Metal. So far it's about 220,000 lines of C++ and 24,000 lines of shaders. No marketplace plugins, premade gameplay systems or templates.

The workflow:

* Claude Code + Opus 5.5 writes all the code. It implements the architecture I lay out, builds the gameplay systems, runs automated tests, reads the results, records gameplay videos and iterates on its own. It also drives Blender to create and edit 3D models.
* Codex: occasional optimizations and the asset generation pipeline.
* GPT Image 2.5: textures and their material maps. Opus calls it through Codex, so textures are part of the automated loop.
* Tripo AI: so far only the player character and their hair. Every other model in the video was made by Opus in Blender.
* Suno: music.

From existing packs I only took some animations and sound effects. The sounds are free placeholders for now, and the music is still a work in progress. The airship models are rough too: the whole set of them came from a single prompt, which is why they look so basic and don't always make sense, like where the balloon is attached. Opus and I haven't spent any time on them yet.

I knew going in what these tools can do, and I picked each one for the job it does best. So the process is smooth: I'm not spending my days fixing AI code; mostly I decide what to build next and check that it feels right. Things do break, though. The trickiest bug so far: the same world seed gave different islands on Windows than on macOS, which would break co-op, since every player needs the exact same world. The Windows compiler evaluates function arguments in a different order, so random numbers were drawn in a different sequence. The determinism tests caught it, and Opus found the cause and fixed it. That's the usual loop: the tests catch a problem, the AI finds and fixes it.

It's still early and rough in places. Happy to answer any questions about the setup. And I'm curious: what would you want to see next in the airship fights?

Full gameplay video (10 minutes): [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJSDQuWSayc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJSDQuWSayc)

comments.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
comments.body:
Alex here from Tripo. Really interesting breakdown, especially that Tripo currently only accounts for the player character and hair while the rest of the pipeline is being generated through Blender automation.

That actually makes the comparison more useful because you have a working alternative pipeline rather than evaluating Tripo in isolation.

I’d be curious what made the character a better fit for Tripo while the environments, airships, and other assets stayed in the Claude + Blender workflow.
